title: Oral English: Stress in Two-Syllable Words
summary: The noun/verb stress rule for two-syllable words, with prepositions and a minimal-pairs drill.

p: We do not say every syllable with the same force. A stressed syllable is louder, longer and higher. Wrong stress makes a word sound odd or even changes its meaning, especially in two-syllable words, where stress separates nouns and adjectives from verbs.
Rule 1: most two-syllable nouns and adjectives are stressed on the FIRST syllable: REcord (a disc or account), PREsent (a gift), CONflict (a disagreement), HAPpy, CLEver.
Rule 2: most two-syllable verbs are stressed on the SECOND: reCORD (to write down), preSENT (to give), conFLICT (to clash), deCIDE, beGIN.
Rule 3: most two-syllable prepositions are stressed on the second: beTWEEN, aBOVE, aCROSS.
'The INcrease in prices will inCREASE our costs.' 'There was a REbel in the army. The soldiers decided to reBEL.' Pairs: CONduct / conDUCT; PROduce / proDUCE; OBject / obJECT; PERmit / perMIT.

activity: Mark the stress and give the word class: project, desert, suspect (noun first-syllable stress, verb second-syllable stress); contest, insult, progress, protest, extract. Write two sentences using 'content' as a noun and as a verb and mark the stress (CONtent, conTENT).

title: Comprehension: Paraphrasing Poems and Dramatic Works
summary: How to turn dense or old-fashioned poetry and drama into plain modern prose, with a table of archaic words, a worked example from Julius Caesar and a stanza of Blake.

p: To paraphrase is to restate a text in your own words. Poems and older plays (such as Shakespeare's) use old words, tangled word order and dense figures. Paraphrasing turns them into clear modern prose.

Step 1: read the whole stanza or speech for the overall sense and mood. Step 2: work line by line: translate old words (thou, thee, thy, thine = you, your, yours; art = are; hast = have; dost = do; hath = has; wherefore = why: 'Wherefore art thou Romeo?' means 'Why are you Romeo?', not 'Where are you?'); untangle figures (metaphor 'All the world's a stage' = life is like a theatre performance; simile 'My love is like a red, red rose' = his love is beautiful and delicate; personification 'The wind whispered through the trees' = the wind blew softly with a whispering sound). Step 3: restate the literal meaning in simple sentences; ignore rhyme and rhythm.
Also identify theme (love, power, betrayal, time), mood (melancholic, joyful, tense), imagery (language that appeals to the senses) and dramatic features: dialogue, monologue and stage directions.

'Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears; I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him. The evil that men do lives after them; the good is oft interred with their bones.' 'Lend me your ears' is an idiom for 'listen to me'. Paraphrase: 'My fellow citizens, please listen. I have come to bury Caesar, not to praise him. People are remembered for the bad they did, while the good is often forgotten when they die.' Theme: the fickleness of opinion and the nature of legacy.

William Blake's 'The Tyger' opens: 'Tyger Tyger, burning bright, / In the forests of the night; / What immortal hand or eye, / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?' A paraphrase: 'Tiger, shining like fire in the dark forests, what divine being could have made you so awesome and so perfectly formed?' Imagery: 'burning bright'. A metaphor: the tiger as a burning fire.

activity: Paraphrase 'He was a lion in the battle' (He fought with great courage and ferocity). Explain 'wherefore' (why). What is the difference between a monologue and stage directions? (A monologue is a long speech by a character; stage directions are the playwright's instructions about movement, setting and tone.)

title: Grammar: Concord (Subject-Verb Agreement)
summary: Eight rules of concord: basic agreement, compound subjects with 'and', 'or' and 'nor', indefinite pronouns, collective nouns, 'there is/are', intervening phrases, and titles and quantities.

p: A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb. 'The boy runs.' 'The boys run.'
1. Compound subjects joined by 'and' are usually plural: 'Tola and Bola are here.' Exception: two nouns that name one thing: 'Rice and beans is my favourite meal.'
2. With 'or' or 'nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject (proximity rule): 'Neither the teacher nor the students are late.' 'Neither the students nor the teacher is late.'

3. These indefinite pronouns are singular: each, every, either, neither, one, no one, everyone, someone, anyone, nobody, everybody, somebody, anybody, nothing, everything, something, anything: 'Everyone has a pen.'

4. Collective nouns (team, committee, family, class, government, staff): singular when the group acts as one ('The team is winning'); plural when members act separately, more usual in British English ('The committee are arguing among themselves').
5. 'There is' or 'There are' agrees with the subject that follows: 'There is a book on the table.' 'There are many books on the table.'
6. Phrases such as as well as, along with, together with and in addition to do not change the number: 'The manager, as well as the assistants, is responsible.'
7. Titles of books, films and countries are singular: 'The Brothers Karamazov is a long novel.'
8. Amounts seen as one sum are singular: 'Ten thousand naira is a lot of money.' Subjects such as mathematics and news are singular: 'Mathematics is a challenging subject.'

activity: Choose: (a) The list of ingredients (is/are) on the back (is); (b) The jury (has/have) reached its verdict (has, or have in British usage when members differ); (c) One of my friends (is/are) going to London (is); (d) There (is/are) a pen, a book and a notebook on the desk (is, agreeing with the nearer item, or are); (e) Mathematics (is/are) a challenging subject (is). Write five sentences showing five different rules.

title: Oral English: Vowel Contrasts
summary: Short and long vowels /ɪ/ and /iː/, /ʊ/ and /uː/, /æ/ and /ɑː/ with minimal pairs and sentences.

p: Vowels are made with an open vocal tract. The difference between short and long vowels is not only length but also the tongue position and mouth shape. Mispronouncing them causes misunderstanding because many words form minimal pairs.

/ɪ/ as in 'sit': short and relaxed, tongue in the centre-front: ship, slip, bin, hit, grin, sin. /iː/ as in 'seat': long and tense, tongue high and front, lips slightly spread: sheep, sleep, bean, heat, green, scene. 'Don't slip on the deck of the ship.' 'The sheep are sleeping.' 'I feel fit.' 'I have sore feet.'

/ʊ/ as in 'pull': short, tongue high and back but relaxed, lips slightly rounded: pull, full, could, wood, book, look. /uː/ as in 'pool': long and tense, lips tightly rounded: pool, fool, cool, shoe, blue, food. 'The pull of the current was strong.' 'Let's swim in the pool.' 'Look at that!' 'His name is Luke.'

/æ/ as in 'cat': short, jaw open, tongue low and front: man, cat, bat, hat, pack, sad. /ɑː/ as in 'cart': long, jaw open, tongue low and drawn back: mark, cart, barn, heart, park, calm. 'The cat sat on the mat.' 'We put the shopping in the cart.' 'He wore a hat.' 'She has a kind heart.'

title: Structure: Adjuncts, Conjuncts and Disjuncts
summary: Three kinds of adverbial: adjuncts that modify the verb, conjuncts that link ideas and disjuncts that comment on a whole sentence.

p: Adverbials add information. They fall into three types by function.

Part of the core of the clause; they modify the verb and tell us how, when, where, how often or why. Remove one and the sentence is still complete but loses detail. Manner: 'He ran quickly.' Place: 'She is sitting in the garden.' Time: 'We will leave tomorrow.' Frequency: 'He often visits his grandparents.' Reason: 'He left because he was tired.'

Not part of the core meaning; they connect sentences or clauses logically. They show addition (furthermore, moreover), contrast (however), result (therefore) or sequence (meanwhile, first, next). They are usually set off by a comma: 'He is rich; moreover, he is generous.' 'However, he did not agree.' 'Therefore, the project was cancelled.'

Stand outside the core and give the speaker's attitude or judgment about the whole statement. Honesty: frankly, honestly. Judgment: obviously, clearly. Evaluation: luckily, unfortunately, surprisingly. Style: briefly. Usually set off by a comma: 'Luckily, no one was hurt.' 'Surprisingly, he passed the exam.'

activity: Write a sentence for each: adjunct of place (outside), adjunct of time (yesterday), conjunct (however), disjunct (fortunately). Classify: 'He answered the question honestly' (adjunct); 'Therefore, we must take action' (conjunct); 'She will arrive in the morning' (adjunct); 'Sadly, the old theatre is closing down' (disjunct).

title: Comprehension: Simple, Compound and Complex Sentences
summary: How to recognise the three basic sentence structures and why mixing them improves flow and readability.

p: Advanced reading includes noticing how sentences are built. Seeing structure helps you follow how ideas are linked and improves your own writing.

Simple sentence: one independent clause (a subject and a verb giving a complete thought). It may have a compound subject or verb, but only one clause: 'The dog barked.' 'Tola and Bola studied for the exam and passed.'

Compound sentence: two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so: FANBOYS) or a semicolon; the ideas are equally important: 'The dog barked, and the cat ran away.' 'I wanted to go to the party, but I was too tired.' 'She is intelligent; she is also hardworking.'

Complex sentence: one independent clause and at least one dependent clause, which cannot stand alone; it often starts with because, since, although, when, if, after, before, which, that or who: 'The dog barked when the postman arrived.' 'Although it was raining, we went for a walk.' 'This is the book that I recommended.'

activity: Pick a paragraph from a textbook or novel. Copy it, list one simple, one compound and one complex sentence from it, and say how the mix affects its flow and readability.

title: Writing: the Expository Essay
summary: A planned expository essay on how to improve family functioning, with brainstorming, a full outline and the task.

p: An expository essay explains or informs in a clear, logical and objective way. It does not argue a point or tell a story. It presents facts, statistics, examples and explanations in a balanced way, in a neutral tone.

sections.h: Brainstorm and outline: 'How to improve family functioning'
p: Brainstorm: communication, mutual respect, quality time, shared responsibilities, financial planning, conflict resolution, love and support. Choose the three strongest.

Title: 'The Pillars of a Functional Family'. Introduction: hook (the family is the basic unit of society); context (all families face challenges, but a well-functioning one overcomes them); thesis ('A family's strength can be greatly improved by open communication, mutual respect and quality time together').

Body 1, open communication: topic sentence ('The cornerstone of a healthy family is open and honest communication'); explanation (builds trust, prevents misunderstanding, solves problems); examples (family meetings, listening without judgement, a safe place to speak). Body 2, mutual respect: valuing opinions, privacy and differences; respecting boundaries, avoiding harsh criticism, celebrating achievements. Body 3, quality time: love is shown by shared experience; meals without distraction, outings, joint projects, traditions.
Conclusion: restate the thesis in new words; recap the three pillars; end with a hopeful sentence about a happy, supportive family.

activity: Write a 350 to 400-word expository essay on 'How to improve family functioning' with a thesis, at least three body paragraphs (each with a topic sentence and supporting details) and a strong conclusion.

title: Structure: Prepositional Phrases
summary: What a prepositional phrase is and how it works as an adjective (which? what kind?) or as an adverb (where? when? how? why?), with worked examples.

p: A preposition shows a relationship of time, space or logic. A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition and ends with a noun or pronoun (its object). It works as one unit that modifies.

It modifies a noun by answering 'Which one?' or 'What kind?' and usually stands right after the noun. 'The house on the hill has a beautiful view.' (Which house?) 'I admire a person with a sense of humour.' (What kind?) 'The suggestion from the committee was accepted.'

It modifies a verb, adjective or adverb by answering where, when, how or why, and can stand at the start, middle or end. 'We will meet at the restaurant.' (where) 'The concert starts in the evening.' (when) 'She completed the task with incredible speed.' (how) 'He went to the market for some bread.' (why)

'The book on the shelf in the library is by my favourite author': 'on the shelf' (which book?), 'in the library' (which shelf?) and 'by my favourite author' (what kind of book?) are all adjectival. 'The dog slept under the table' (where? adverbial, modifies 'slept'). 'The dog under the table is sleeping' (which dog? adjectival, modifies 'dog').
